summary:
Namibia presents trans visitors with a legal floor that is more workable than the political rhetoric suggests, but with a documented gap between court rulings and administrative practice. The Supreme Court ordered the government in May 2023 to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the Immigration Act. Compliance has failed: immigration officials tell litigant Daniel Digashu that the ruling covers only the couples who brought the case, and he is issued a visitor's visa on every exit. Gender-recognition orders are applied only to the named applicants rather than to "all persons".

Parliament answered the litigation with a package of hostile marriage bills, and reporting that amplified the non-implementation, according to an op-ed by Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre published by the Washington Blade on 22 May 2024. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre characterises implementation of pro-equality rulings as unsatisfactory.

Documentary rules are comparatively workable. Section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 permits a change of gender marker on medical evidence; the Legal Assistance Centre described the process in 2015 as handled case by case and "not problematic". Article 10 of the Namibian Constitution omits gender identity and sexual orientation from its protected grounds, although the UN Human Rights Committee has read the constitutional phrase "other status" as covering them, and in 2016 it recommended legislation prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The state of criminalisation is contested across the sources. A UNDP report of December 2024 states that Namibia's courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024 and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, with implementation contested. Other accounts hold that the High Court declined in 2024 to strike down the common-law offence against men. Mambaonline reported in May 2018 that the colonial-era sodomy law remained on the books but was not believed to have been used since independence in 1990.

Public presence is visible and tolerated. Dozens marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December 2018 in what was described as the biggest LGBTI Pride event held in Namibia to that date. Out-Right Namibia opened Outreach Health, the country's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, at 30 Lister Street in Windhoek West on 17 May 2018, offering HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, and mental, sexual and reproductive health services, with legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations planned. Its director, Friedel Dausab, called it a first.

Organised hostility is also part of the political environment. A Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched in 2014 carrying identical branding, T-shirts and berets, but with an explicitly anti-gay stance that the South African original does not hold.
tangentialFactors:
Namibia's courts have moved ahead of its legislature. The 2023 Supreme Court recognition ruling and the reported 2024 decriminalisation sit against a parliamentary response composed of hostile marriage bills, so the direction of travel in the judiciary and in politics runs in opposite directions.

The country is assessed against a regional framework, the African Commission's Resolution 275 on protection against violence and other human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, which the UNDP marked ten years of in December 2024. Namibia's litigation is conducted by the Southern Africa Litigation Centre, a regional litigator, and its rulings are read against that continental standard.

Public visibility has been demonstrated rather than merely permitted: the December 2018 pride marches in two cities and the opening of a dedicated health centre in Windhoek in the same year indicate an organised community able to operate in daylight. The 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations and the 2015 Legal Assistance Centre assessment of marker changes point the same way.

Counter-currents are documented as well. The 2014 launch of an explicitly anti-gay political movement, the hostile parliamentary bills, and the reported misleading media coverage of the non-implementation show that hostility is organised and public, not incidental.

Friedel Dausab, the organisation's director, described it as a first.

Residents have organised public pride events: marches in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December 2018 drew dozens and were described as the largest such event in Namibia to that date. outOfScopeNotes:
The sources contradict each other on criminalisation. The UNDP report of December 2024 states that Namibian courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024, while other accounts in the inventory state that the High Court declined in 2024 to strike down the common-law offence against men. Which is the operative position, and whether any appeal followed, is unresolved here.

Whether the Supreme Court's May 2023 Immigration Act ruling has since been complied with is unresolved. The Washington Blade op-ed of 22 May 2024 documents non-compliance at that date; no later source in the inventory reports either compliance or continued refusal.

Whether gender-recognition orders have been generalised beyond named applicants, and whether the hostile marriage bills introduced in parliament were enacted, defeated or withdrawn, is not sourced.

Whether the colonial-era sodomy law remains on the statute book after the reported 2024 proceedings is not sourced; the statement that it has not been used since 1990 dates from May 2018.

No source in the inventory addresses entry screening, customs or border questioning of trans travellers, nor whether a visitor's passport gender marker affects visa issuance beyond the treatment of the named litigant.
